message.content:
Triangulation metrics are quantitative measures that describe the quality, performance, and characteristics of a triangulation run.  
In practice they help you understand how well a set of points has been connected into triangles, how accurate the resulting mesh is, and whether it meets the requirements of your application (e.g., GIS, finite‑element analysis, computer graphics, etc.).  

Typical triangulation metrics include:

| Metric | What it tells you | Typical use |
|--------|-------------------|-------------|
| **Number of triangles** | Total count of triangles produced. | Quick sanity check – too few may mean under‑sampling, too many may indicate over‑fitting or inefficiency. |
| **Average triangle area** | Mean area of all triangles. | Indicates overall resolution; smaller areas mean finer detail. |
| **Minimum/maximum triangle area** | Extremes of triangle sizes. | Detects outliers—very small triangles can cause numerical instability, very large ones may miss detail. |
| **Aspect ratio** | Ratio of longest side to shortest altitude. | Measures shape quality; high aspect ratios (elongated triangles) can degrade interpolation accuracy. |
| **Minimum angle** | Smallest internal angle across all triangles. | A low minimum angle often signals poorly shaped triangles that can lead to numerical errors. |
| **Maximum angle** | Largest internal angle. | Helps detect obtuse triangles that might affect mesh quality. |
| **Edge length distribution** | Histogram of edge lengths. | Useful for detecting irregular spacing or clustering of points. |
| **Coverage / fill factor** | Fraction of the target area actually covered by triangles. | Ensures no gaps in the mesh. |
| **Error metrics** | Difference between the triangulated surface and a reference (e.g., ground truth). | Quantifies accuracy of the triangulation. |
| **Runtime / computational cost** | Time taken to generate the triangulation. | Performance benchmarking. |
| **Memory usage** | Peak memory consumption during triangulation. | Resource planning. |

When you run a triangulation algorithm (e.g., Delaunay, constrained Delaunay, or custom mesh generators), the software typically outputs a set of these metrics so you can evaluate whether the mesh satisfies your quality thresholds. In many systems, you can also set tolerances or constraints that influence these metrics—for example, specifying a maximum allowable triangle area or a minimum angle constraint.

In short, triangulation metrics give you a snapshot of the mesh’s geometric fidelity, numerical stability, and computational efficiency, enabling you to tweak your triangulation parameters or point distribution to achieve the desired outcome.
